generation.final_prompt:
Rendering style:
Create an authored editorial illustration for a serious technology newspaper.

Direction:
- authored editorial print language
- deliberate simplified shapes with clear focal hierarchy
- restrained limited palette
- subtle physical print texture
- controlled abstraction and strong negative space
- non-photorealistic but factually grounded representation
- newspaper and social-card readability

Fixed factual and safety restrictions:
- Do not render visible text, captions, headlines, or newspaper typography.
- Do not render logos or trademarks.
- Do not fabricate visible factual evidence.
- Do not render interfaces or screenshots.
- Do not imitate a named or living artist.

Profile-specific exclusions:
- glossy CGI
- luxury product render
- generic futuristic concept art
- cyberpunk or neon
- glowing circuit-board decoration
- floating particles
- heroic centered hardware
- server rack treated as monument or skyscraper
- generic server room
- advertising composition
- airbrushed gradients
- synthetic chrome
- excessive pseudo-technical detail
- malformed or visible text
- labels
- diagrams with words

Exact source facts:
Title: N-ABLE PATCHES MAX-SEVERITY N-CENTRAL FLAW AMID ONGOING ATTACKS
Summary: Unauthenticated attackers can execute code on internet-exposed N-central RMM servers through a low-complexity attack exploiting CVE-2026-86218. Huntress has flagged it as a potential zero-day after finding a compromised customer instance whose logs had already rotated. Shadowserver counts nearly 1,500 exposed N-central servers, most in the United States and Europe. On-premises operators need N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4 immediately, since HF3 systems remain vulnerable to this flaw despite last week's fixes for the authentication-bypass pair CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207.

Editorial idea:
An internet-facing management system can become an entry point for attackers before defenders have time to respond.

Central subject:
The actively exploited N-central vulnerability and the exposed systems it threatens.

Visual relationship:
A public-facing control point connects directly to unauthorized code execution, showing how a low-complexity flaw can bypass authentication and reach a managed environment.

Composition:
A narrow service doorway stands open at the edge of an office floor, with an intruder's shadow crossing the threshold while defenders inside examine incomplete records; keep the scene grounded in physical access and exposure rather than depicting generic cyber imagery.

Permitted literal elements:
an open doorway labeled only by architectural context, not rendered text
a small access-control panel left bypassed
an interior operations room with several workstations
a partially erased incident log on a desk
a shadow crossing from outside into the room

Abstraction level:
medium

Story-specific forbidden elements:
racks
chips
laptops as isolated hero objects
robots
clouds
shields
arrows
charts
skyscrapers
chess
handshakes
split-screen conflict
logos
rendered text
unsupported malware details

Likely failure modes to avoid:
Do not depict the vulnerability as a physical explosion or dramatic destruction.
Do not imply that every exposed server has been compromised.
Do not add a specific attacker identity, payload, or geographic setting beyond the reported exposure

Global factual restrictions:
Do not fabricate visible factual evidence. Do not imitate a named or living artist. Do not render interfaces or screenshots.
Do not render any words, letters, numbers, labels, captions, annotations, signage, diagrams with text, logos, watermarks, or pseudo-writing anywhere in the image.
If the concept cannot be represented without visible text, represent the relationship through shape, scale, spacing, direction, grouping, interruption, containment, or contrast instead.
